text: You get a binary string s, and two integers, min jump and max jump. You start at index zero, and the first character is always a zero. From index i, you can jump to index j, as long as j is at least i plus min jump, at most i plus max jump, not past the end of the string, and the character at j is a zero. Return true if you can reach the last index.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a one is a wall. I can never land on it. A zero is a spot I can land on. And every jump is at least min jump and at most max jump to the right. I never move left. Is that right?

Good. Then I want to flip the question around. Instead of asking where can I go from i, I'll ask: who can jump into i? A cell j can reach i only if j sits in the range from i minus max jump up to i minus min jump. So index i is reachable when its character is a zero, and at least one reachable cell sits in that range. That range is the whole problem. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Length is from two up to ten to the fifth. Each character is a zero or a one. And min jump is at least one, at most max jump, and max jump is less than the length.

Okay. So max jump can be almost as big as n. That matters for the cost — I'll come back to it. Let me run through the example. The string is zero one one zero one zero, min jump two, max jump three. From index zero, I can jump to two or three. Index two is a wall, index three is open. From three, I can jump to five. Index five is the last one, and it's a zero. So the path is zero, to three, to five, and the answer is true. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be a dp array where each index scans its whole range for one true cell. That's correct, but it costs n times the window width — with all zeros and max jump ninety-nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine, it took about one point eight seconds when I measured it. Way too slow. This problem reminds me of a sliding window. When i moves right by one, the range moves right by one: exactly one cell enters on the right, at i minus min jump, and one drops off on the left, at i minus max jump minus one. So I don't rescan — I just update a running number. I'll go with the sliding-window DP: one pass, constant work per step.

Here's the plan. Dp of i means I can stand on index i, and the start is true. Cnt is how many true dp values sit in the window. First, for each i from min jump, count the cell entering at i minus min jump. Second, uncount the cell leaving at i minus max jump minus one, if it exists. Third, dp of i is true when cnt is above zero and the character is a zero. One thing worth flagging — it has to be a count, not a flag. When one reachable cell leaves, a flag goes false even if another is still inside. A flag passes both examples but fails three zeros with jumps one and one. A farthest-pointer B F S is also linear, but the count is easier to prove. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop from min jump to n minus one, doing exactly the three plan steps: count the entering cell, uncount the leaving cell, then set dp of i from the count and the character. Cells before min jump just stay false. One thing worth flagging — the remove guard checks at least zero, not strictly above zero. With the strict version, the start cell never leaves the window, so it keeps helping cells it can't really reach: zero one zero, with jumps one and one, returns true, but the answer is false. The zero check on the character matters the same way — without it, the string zero one would mark a wall as reachable.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Example one: zero one one zero one zero, jumps two and three, expected true. The key row is i equals four: the start cell slides out of the window, so cnt drops to zero — the window really forgets old cells. Then at i equals five, dp of three enters, cnt is one, and index five is a zero. So true, along zero, three, five. Example two returns false, because index three, the only reachable cell, leaves the window right at the last index. Corner cases: zero then one, false — the last cell is a wall. Four zeros with a fixed jump of two, false — no wall, but parity only lands on even indices.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is linear — each index does one add check and one remove check. The space complexity is linear, for the dp array. On the naive scan's worst case the window holds almost a hundred thousand cells, yet this version took about a hundred and five microseconds instead of one point eight seconds, because the window size never shows up in the cost. Oh, one more thing — I return the last dp value, not whether the counter is above zero. The counter ignores whether the last cell is a wall, so zero one, with jumps one and one, would wrongly give true. That bug also passes both examples, so it's easy to miss.
Good. Could you do it without the window count?

Two ways. First, breadth-first search with a farthest pointer: from each reachable index I scan its jump range, but start from the farthest index already checked, so every index is looked at once. On the same worst case it ran in about a hundred and eighteen microseconds, about the same as the DP. Second, prefix sums: keep a running count of true dp values, and the window check becomes one subtraction. It's the same counter, written as a range sum. Also, a vector of bools is much smaller — about twelve and a half thousand bytes versus four hundred thousand — but it was about three times slower in my run, so I kept the vector of ints.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You flipped the question to, who can jump into i, which turned a graph search into a window that slides one step at a time. You explained why the window needs a count, not a flag, and backed it with the three-zeros case — a bug that passes both examples. And you showed that the remove guard, the character check, and returning the last dp value are each correctness rules, with a small input that breaks each one. Good work.
